title: Why does sunset line up with Manhattan’s streets?
checkedAgainst: Skyfield 1.55 observing the Sun through JPL’s DE440s ephemeris, recorded by `oracle/sun.py` into `fixtures/henge-sun.json`: the model’s solar position at 74 instants, day and night, to 0.015°; its half- and full-Sun moments on every evening of 2026 at both places to 5 seconds and 0.01°; and its alignment evenings, exactly. The places are OpenStreetMap nodes and each street’s bearing GeographicLib 2.1’s WGS84 geodesic between two of them, recorded in the same fixture. The Hayden Planetarium’s published 2026 minutes are a cross-check: at each the ephemeris puts the Sun 0.12°–0.20° north of 42nd Street, and its dates fall two to four days nearer the solstice than a flat horizon gives. The globe's coastlines are Natural Earth 1:110m (v5.1.2), written to `land.ts` by `oracle/land.py`. The idealised sky is checked against 48 vectors from ERFA’s `hd2ae` (pyerfa 2.0.1.5, `oracle/henge.py`, `fixtures/henge-erfa.json`) and USNO’s altitude formula. All in `model.test.ts`; `scene.test.ts` checks the pictures against the model.

answer: The street stays fixed while Earth’s tilt moves the sunset direction across it and back

questions.question: Another city’s streets point 10° north of west, between Manhattan’s 29° and due west. Are its two alignment seasons nearer the June solstice than Manhattan’s, or farther from it?
questions.answer: Farther from it. The sunset direction sweeps north from December to June and back; it passes 10° north of west before it reaches 29° on the way north, and after it on the way back, so the two seasons sit nearer the equinoxes.

questions.question: Suppose another street points farther north than the northernmost sunset at its latitude. How many low-Sun alignments does it get?
questions.answer: None. The annual curve must cross the street’s direction. Moving the street beyond its northern turning point removes both crossings.

steps.title: Why does the Sun line up on so few evenings?
steps.line: Predict: will the low Sun line up again tomorrow?
steps.caption: Stand on the Tudor City overpass and look west down 42nd Street. At 8:14 pm on 25 May 2026 the setting Sun sat half above the horizon in the slot between the buildings, drawn true size. The Hayden Planetarium calls this Manhattanhenge. The street points the same way all year, so what changes must be where the Sun sets.
steps.picture: Looking down the street, five degrees either side, between two walls of buildings: the half Sun on 25 May, 0.11° left of the street’s line.

steps.title: A week either side, the Sun sets behind the buildings
steps.line: Half Sun on four evenings of 2026, true size, seen from one spot.
steps.caption: The street stays fixed while Earth’s tilt moves the sunset direction across it and back. The next evening, 26 May, half Sun stood 0.24° farther right, partly out of a slot 0.65° wide. A week before, it set 2.0° left; a week after, 1.4° right: behind the buildings, dashed. On 18 March, when Randolph Street in Chicago lines up, it set 29.4° left.

state.legend: Half Sun, true size. Dashed: behind the buildings

legend.after: Half Sun, true size. Dashed: behind the buildings

steps.picture: Looking down the street, five degrees either side, between two walls of buildings: the half Sun on 18 May, 2.02° left of the street’s line; the half Sun on 25 May, 0.11° left of the street’s line; the half Sun on 26 May, 0.13° right of the street’s line; the half Sun on 1 June, 1.40° right of the street’s line. Off to the side: 18 March, 29.4° left of the street’s line.

steps.title: From above: sunset lines up with 42nd Street, sunrise does not
steps.line: North is up; the grid is schematic. Gold arrows: the Sun at sunset and sunrise on an alignment day.
steps.caption: From above, 42nd Street points 29.0° north of west, measured between two OpenStreetMap points 2.7 km apart, and the same angle south of east at the other end. On an alignment evening the setting Sun lies on that line. That morning it rose 29.0° north of east, 58.1° from the street’s other end, which faces the sunrise only on winter mornings around the December solstice.

legend.before: Half Sun, true size. Dashed: behind the buildings

steps.picture: Sunset. 29.0° north of west. Sunrise. 29.0° north of east. N. East end. 29.0° south of east. Sunrise misses that end by 58.1°.

steps.title: The Sun sets toward the place where it stands overhead
steps.line: Earth from space: the place, its street carried on, and where the Sun is overhead.
steps.caption: At any moment the Sun stands overhead at one point on Earth, and from New York it sets toward that point once the point is a quarter of the way round the globe away. At 8:14 pm on 25 May it was overhead at 21.1° N, over the Pacific, where 42nd Street, carried on along the ground, meets that ring. Through the year the point slides between the tropics, crossing the street’s line twice.
steps.picture: Earth from space, with New York on it. A red line carries the street on along the ground to a gold ring a quarter of the way round the globe, meeting it at 21.2° north. The Sun stands overhead on that ring at half Sun: on 25 May at 21.1° north, on 18 March at 0.7° south.

steps.title: June’s Sun sets 31.7° north of west, December’s 31.7° south
steps.line: Red: the street’s arc, rising from the horizon where the street points, 29.0° north of west.
steps.caption: New York’s sky as a dome, seen from outside, west of it. Each day the Sun’s centre goes round a circle about the celestial pole; the bold arc is its day, ending at a flat horizon. June’s circle lies more above the horizon and ends 31.7° north of west, 2.6° beyond the street. December’s shorter path ends 31.7° south of west, far short of it. The circle shifts because Earth’s axis is tilted.
steps.picture: N. S. W. December. Equinox. June. Street. Pole. New York’s horizon.

steps.title: Follow the sunset through a year
steps.line: Predict: how many times will the sunset cross the street?
steps.caption: Now let a year run, from the December solstice to the next. The Sun’s daily circle slides north, and its sunset, the gold band along the horizon, travels north with it. It passes the street, turns back in June, and passes it again. One fixed direction, crossed on the way out and on the way back. These circles come from an idealised circular orbit.
steps.picture: The dome with one day’s path. Its Sun sets 31.7° south of west. Since the December solstice the sunset has crossed the street twice.

steps.title: Across the street in May, back across it in July
steps.line: Change the place: the street turns, and the crossings move.
steps.caption: Every evening of 2026 as a chart: across, January to December; up, how far north along the horizon the half Sun sets, from the ephemeris. The line labelled 42nd Street stays at its bearing. The curve crosses it on 25 May and 16 July. Chicago’s Randolph Street points due west, so the same curve crosses it in March and September. The place changes the direction we wait for, not Earth’s motion.
steps.picture: Gold: the half Sun’s direction, 2026. due west. Jan. Apr. Jul. Oct. Dec. 42nd Street. 25 May. 16 July.

steps.title: One axis direction, opposite sides of the Sun
steps.line: Why the Sun’s daily circle shifts: Earth’s tilt, seen from beside its orbit.
steps.caption: Earth’s axis keeps nearly the same direction through the year. In June the north leans sunward; in December it leans away. The red dot is New York at noon, on the circle Earth’s daily turn carries it round: gold where that circle is in sunlight, dark where it is in night. In June 62% of the circle is in sunlight, in December 38%. Sizes and distances here are schematic.
steps.picture: Sun. N. N. June. December. North sunward. North away. Red dot: New York at noon, on its daily circle. Gold: the circle in daylight; dark: in night.

steps.title: From the sky to the street: bearing and height in one view
steps.line: Stand at the dome’s centre and lower your eyes along the street.
steps.caption: Stand in the street, at the dome’s centre, and lower your eyes along the street’s circle to the horizon: the street views earlier are this view, narrowed. From the centre, the street’s circle, the horizon and the buildings’ edges stay straight, as a camera sees them. Left and right say whether the Sun is centred between the buildings; up and down say how much of its disc is above the horizon. The buildings and disc here are schematic.
steps.picture: Looking along the street from its middle, 3° above the horizon: the street’s circle runs straight up the middle, and the Sun’s path on a May evening comes down to the horizon where the street points, with the Sun’s centre on the horizon.

steps.title: Half Sun and full Sun: two moments, one slot
steps.line: True size, a degree either side of the street.
steps.caption: Half Sun puts the Sun’s centre on the flat horizon; full Sun puts its lower edge there. Down one street that needs a Sun a little farther north, so in May full Sun comes later: half on 25 May at 8:14 pm, full on 27 May at 8:14 pm. In July the order reverses. The Hayden Planetarium publishes 28 and 29 May, 11 and 12 July, nearer the solstice, as a horizon raised above this flat one gives.
steps.picture: Two close views down the street at true size. Left: half Sun on 25 May at 8:14 pm, its centre on the horizon in the slot between the buildings. Right: full Sun on 27 May at 8:14 pm, its lower edge on the horizon.
